name: Z80 Assembly
title: Z80 assembly, register by register
intro: The Zilog Z80 is an 8-bit processor from 1976 that powered the ZX Spectrum, MSX computers, the TRS-80, CP/M business machines and the Game Boy's close cousin. Assembly language is a readable spelling of the processor's own instructions, so every line does one small, exact thing. This course writes small programs for CP/M, the disk operating system most Z80 business machines ran, because CP/M gives you an easy way to print text. To run them, assemble a file with an assembler such as pasmo, z80asm or sjasmplus into a .COM file, then start it inside a CP/M emulator such as RunCPM. Every complete program here shows exactly what it prints.

lessons.title: Registers and LD
lessons.summary: The processor's own tiny variables, and moving data between them.

sections.p: The Z80 has a handful of 8-bit registers: A (the accumulator, where most arithmetic happens), B, C, D, E, H and L. They pair up into 16-bit registers BC, DE and HL, which usually hold addresses. 8 bits hold 0–255; 16 bits hold 0–65535, the whole memory map.

sections.code:
LD   A, 5        ; A = 5
        LD   B, A        ; B = 5 too
        LD   HL, 8000h   ; HL = address 8000 (hex)
        LD   (HL), A     ; memory[8000h] = 5
        LD   A, (HL)     ; A = memory[8000h]
sections.p: LD destination, source copies a value. The destination always comes first. Brackets mean “the memory at this address”.

sections.code:
LD   A, 65       ; decimal
        LD   A, 41h      ; the same, in hex
        LD   A, 01000001b ; the same, in binary
        LD   A, 'A'      ; the same, as a character
sections.p: Assembly programmers write numbers in whichever base is clearest. 255, 0FFh and 11111111b are the same value. A hex number that starts with a letter needs a leading 0 so the assembler does not mistake it for a name. A character in quotes, like 'A', means its code: 65.

sections.code:
LD   HL, 1234h   ; H = 12h, L = 34h
        LD   L, 0        ; HL is now 1200h
        LD   DE, 300     ; 300 = 012Ch, so D = 01h, E = 2Ch
sections.p: H is the high byte of HL and L the low byte. Changing one changes the pair. The same goes for B/C and D/E.

practice.why: LD copies the source (A, holding 5) into the destination (B).
practice.q: After LD A, 5 then LD B, A, what is in B?

practice.why: The destination comes first, and brackets mean memory at that address.
options: Stores A into memory at the address in HL
practice.answer: Stores A into memory at the address in HL

practice.why: H is the high byte of the pair, L the low byte.
practice.q: HL holds 1234h. What is in H?

practice.why: 10h, 16 and 00010000b are all sixteen; 0Ah is ten.
practice.q: Which value is not the same as the others?

practice.why: A word that starts with a letter looks like a label; the leading 0 marks it as a number.
options: So the assembler reads a number, not a name
practice.answer: So the assembler reads a number, not a name

practice.why: Changing L only replaces the low byte; H stays 80h, so HL becomes 8005h.
practice.q: After LD HL, 8000h then LD L, 5, what is in HL?

practice.why: Brackets mean memory; the destination A comes first, so A receives the byte.
options: Loads A from the memory byte HL points at
Stores A into memory at HL
practice.answer: Loads A from the memory byte HL points at

lessons.title: Hello, CP/M
lessons.summary: The shape of a whole program, and printing with the BDOS.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   DE, msg     ; DE = address of the text
        LD   C, 9        ; BDOS function 9: print string
        CALL 5
        RET              ; back to CP/M
msg:    DB   'Hello, squirrel!$'
sections.p: A CP/M program is loaded at address 100h, so it starts with ORG 100h. To print, you ask the operating system: put a function number in C and CALL 5, the address of the BDOS (Basic Disk Operating System). Function 9 prints the string whose address is in DE, up to a $ sign. RET at the end goes back to CP/M.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   DE, msg
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
msg:    DB   'Line one', 13, 10
        DB   'Line two$'
sections.p: DB (define byte) is not an instruction. It tells the assembler to place bytes right there in the program: characters from quoted text, and numbers as they are. 13 and 10 are carriage return and line feed, which together start a new line on CP/M.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   E, 'O'
        LD   C, 2        ; BDOS function 2: print the character in E
        CALL 5
        LD   E, 'K'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: Function 2 prints the single character in E. The BDOS is allowed to change any register, so set C and E again before every call.

sections.code:
BDOS    EQU  5
PRINT   EQU  9
        ORG  100h
        LD   DE, msg
        LD   C, PRINT
        CALL BDOS
        RET
msg:    DB   'Named and tidy$'
sections.p: name EQU value gives a number a name, so the program says what it means. Labels like msg: are names too: they stand for the address where they appear.

practice.why: Function 9 stops at the first $ and does not print it.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   DE, msg
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
msg:    DB   'Nuts$ and more'

practice.why: CP/M reads the function number from C; DE or E holds what it works on.
practice.q: Which register holds the BDOS function number?

practice.why: Each call to function 2 prints the character in E, in program order.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   E, 'H'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        LD   E, 'I'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: CP/M loads every .COM program at 100h, so labels must be counted from there.
practice.q: What does ORG 100h tell the assembler?
options: The program will be loaded at address 100h
practice.answer: The program will be loaded at address 100h

practice.why: CP/M makes no promise to keep registers, so a careful program reloads them.
practice.q: Why set C again before a second CALL 5?
options: The BDOS may have changed it
It is only needed for style
practice.answer: The BDOS may have changed it

practice.why: 13 and 10 start a new line; function 9 then prints OK and stops at $.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   DE, msg
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
msg:    DB   'Z80', 13, 10
        DB   'OK$'

practice.why: Each function-2 call prints the character currently in E.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   E, 'Z'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        LD   E, '8'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        LD   E, '0'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

lessons.title: Arithmetic and the carry
lessons.summary: ADD, SUB, INC and DEC; the carry flag; 16-bit sums.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 3
        ADD  A, 4        ; A = 7
        SUB  2           ; A = 5
        INC  A           ; A = 6
        ADD  A, '0'      ; A = '6'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: ADD A, x and SUB x work on the accumulator. INC and DEC add or take one from any register. Adding the character code of '0' (48) to a number from 0 to 9 gives the digit to print.

sections.code:
LD   A, 250
        ADD  A, 10       ; A = 4, carry set
        LD   A, 3
        SUB  5           ; A = 254, carry set (borrow)
        LD   A, 255
        INC  A           ; A = 0, carry unchanged
sections.p: An 8-bit register wraps: 250 + 10 is 4, not 260. When that happens the carry flag (C) is set, as if the ninth bit fell out into it. Subtraction that goes below 0 also wraps and sets carry (a “borrow”). INC and DEC wrap too, but leave carry alone.

sections.h: ADC and SBC carry it on
sections.code:
; 300 + 500 using 8-bit steps: 012Ch + 01F4h
        LD   A, 2Ch      ; low byte of 300
        ADD  A, 0F4h     ; low byte of 500: A = 20h, carry set
        LD   L, A
        LD   A, 01h      ; high byte of 300
        ADC  A, 01h      ; high byte of 500, plus the carry: A = 03h
        LD   H, A        ; HL = 0320h = 800
sections.p: ADC (add with carry) adds the carry flag as an extra 1. That is how you add numbers wider than 8 bits: add the low bytes, then ADC the high bytes. SBC does the same for subtraction.

sections.code:
LD   HL, 1000
        LD   DE, 234
        ADD  HL, DE      ; HL = 1234
        OR   A           ; clear the carry flag
        SBC  HL, DE      ; HL = 1000 again
sections.p: ADD HL, rr adds a whole register pair in one go. INC HL and DEC HL step a pointer. There is no 16-bit SUB; use OR A to clear carry and then SBC HL, DE.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 7
        NEG              ; A = 249, which is -7
        ADD  A, 9        ; 249 + 9 wraps to 2
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: NEG turns A into 0 − A. In 8 bits, −1 is written 255, −2 is 254, and so on (two's complement). The same bits can be read as 0 to 255 or as −128 to 127; it is the program that decides which.

practice.why: 9 − 4 is 5, DEC makes it 4, and adding '0' makes the character 4.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 9
        SUB  4
        DEC  A
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: 300 does not fit in 8 bits; it wraps to 300 − 256 = 44 and sets carry.
practice.q: A holds 200. After ADD A, 100, what is in A?

practice.why: ADC means add with carry; it is how wider numbers are added byte by byte.
practice.q: Which instruction adds the carry flag in as well?

practice.why: INC wraps to 0 and sets the zero flag, but it never touches carry.
practice.q: A holds 255 and carry is clear. After INC A?

practice.why: NEG makes A −2 (254); 254 + 7 wraps to 5.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 2
        NEG
        ADD  A, 7
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: SBC subtracts the carry as well; OR A leaves A alone but always clears carry.
practice.q: Why OR A before SBC HL, DE?
options: To clear carry so it is not subtracted too
practice.answer: To clear carry so it is not subtracted too

practice.why: 5 + 3 is 8; INC makes 9; adding '0' makes the character 9.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 5
        ADD  A, 3
        INC  A
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: ADD A, A doubles A: 4 becomes 8.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 4
        ADD  A, A
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

lessons.title: Flags and decisions
lessons.summary: CP, the zero and carry flags, and conditional jumps.

sections.code:
CP   10          ; compare A with 10
        JR   Z, ten      ; jump if A was 10
        JR   C, small    ; jump if A was less than 10
        ; otherwise A is bigger than 10 here
sections.p: Arithmetic sets flags. The most used are Z (the result was zero) and C (carry). CP x compares A with x by subtracting without keeping the answer, only the flags. Jumps then test them: JP Z, JR NZ, JR C, JR NC.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 7
        CP   5
        JR   C, less     ; not taken: 7 is not below 5
        LD   DE, big
        JR   show
less:   LD   DE, small
show:   LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
big:    DB   'big$'
small:  DB   'small$'
sections.p: After CP x: Z set means A = x. C set means A < x (unsigned). Neither set means A > x. NC means A ≥ x.

JR (jump relative) is one byte shorter and can reach about 127 bytes forward or back; it only tests Z, NZ, C and NC. JP reaches anywhere and can also test the sign (P, M) and parity/overflow (PE, PO). Use JR for short hops.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 0        ; try 0, 1 or 2
        CP   0
        JR   NZ, not0
        LD   DE, zero
        JR   done
not0:   CP   1
        JR   NZ, other
        LD   DE, one
        JR   done
other:  LD   DE, many
done:   LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
zero:   DB   'none$'
one:    DB   'one$'
many:   DB   'lots$'
sections.p: A chain of compares makes a decision with several branches. Each branch ends with a jump past the others.

sections.code:
OR   A           ; is A zero?
        JR   Z, empty
        DEC  B           ; DEC sets Z when B reaches 0
        JR   Z, last
sections.p: OR A leaves A unchanged but sets Z if A is 0, so you do not need CP 0. AND A works the same way. Many instructions set flags as a side effect, so you can often jump straight after DEC or SUB.

practice.why: 10 − 10 is zero, so Z is set; there is no borrow, so C is clear.
practice.q: After CP 10 with A = 10, which flag is set?

practice.why: 4 − 10 borrows, setting the carry flag, so A is less than 10.
practice.q: After CP 10 with A = 4, which jump is taken?

practice.why: A equals 3, so Z is set and JR NZ is not taken; E gets Y.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 3
        CP   3
        JR   NZ, no
        LD   E, 'Y'
        JR   say
no:     LD   E, 'N'
say:    LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: 12 − 20 borrows, so carry is set and JR NC is not taken.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 12
        CP   20
        JR   NC, isbig
        LD   DE, lomsg
        JR   say
isbig:  LD   DE, himsg
say:    LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
lomsg:  DB   'low$'
himsg:  DB   'high$'

practice.why: JR only tests Z, NZ, C and NC; the sign condition M needs JP.
practice.q: Which jump cannot be written with JR?

practice.why: A OR A is A; the point is that Z and S now describe A, and carry is cleared.
practice.q: What does OR A do to A?
options: Nothing, but it sets the flags from A
practice.answer: Nothing, but it sets the flags from A

practice.why: A equals 5, so Z is set and JR Z takes the yes branch.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 5
        CP   5
        JR   Z, yes
        LD   E, 'N'
        JR   say
yes:    LD   E, 'Y'
say:    LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: 9 is not below 4, so carry is clear and JR C is skipped.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 9
        CP   4
        JR   C, lo
        LD   DE, hi
        JR   out
lo:     LD   DE, lom
out:    LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
hi:     DB   'hi$'
lom:    DB   'lo$'

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 3        ; loop three times
        LD   A, 0
again:  ADD  A, 2        ; A = 2, 4, 6
        DJNZ again
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: DJNZ label means “decrement B, jump if not zero”. Put the count in B and the loop runs exactly that many times. Here the BDOS call is outside the loop, so nothing else disturbs B.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 5
star:   PUSH BC
        LD   E, '*'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  BC
        DJNZ star
        RET
sections.p: If the loop body calls the BDOS, B may come back changed. PUSH BC before the call and POP BC after keep the counter safe. This loop prints five stars.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   D, '1'
next:   PUSH DE
        LD   E, D
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  DE
        INC  D
        LD   A, D
        CP   '6'         ; stop after 5
        JR   NZ, next
        RET
sections.p: To count up, keep the number in a register, print or use it, add one, and compare with the end value. Here the digit itself is the counter, kept in D and saved around the call.

sections.code:
LD   BC, 1000
slow:   ; ... loop body ...
        DEC  BC
        LD   A, B
        OR   C
        JR   NZ, slow    ; runs 1000 times
sections.p: DJNZ only counts to 256. For more, count down a register pair. DEC BC does not set any flags, so test for zero by hand: LD A, B then OR C sets Z only when both halves are 0.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   D, 3
row:    LD   B, 4
dot:    PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        LD   E, '.'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  DE
        POP  BC
        DJNZ dot
        PUSH DE
        LD   DE, crlf
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        POP  DE
        DEC  D
        JR   NZ, row
        RET
crlf:   DB   13, 10, '$'
sections.p: An inner loop needs its own counter, or the outer counter must be saved. This one prints three rows of four dots, with the outer count in D and the inner count in B.

practice.why: B goes 3 → 2 → 1 → 0; the jump is taken until B reaches 0.
practice.q: How many times does a DJNZ loop run when it starts with LD B, 3?

practice.why: B starts at 4, so the body runs four times.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 4
lp:     PUSH BC
        LD   E, '#'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  BC
        DJNZ lp
        RET

practice.why: ADD A, A doubles: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 over three passes.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 3
        LD   A, 1
lp:     ADD  A, A
        DJNZ lp
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: 16-bit INC and DEC leave the flags alone, so you check both halves for zero yourself.
practice.q: Why test LD A, B / OR C after DEC BC?
options: OR C adds C to B

practice.why: The first DEC turns 0 into 255, so the loop goes all the way round: 256 passes.
practice.q: What does LD B, 0 then a DJNZ loop do?

practice.why: The BDOS may change B; saving BC on the stack and restoring it keeps the counter.
practice.q: The loop body calls the BDOS. What keeps the DJNZ count safe?
options: PUSH BC before, POP BC after
practice.answer: PUSH BC before, POP BC after

practice.why: Two passes add 2 each time: 3 → 5 → 7.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 2
        LD   A, 3
lp:     ADD  A, 2
        DJNZ lp
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: B starts at 3 and PUSH/POP keep it safe across each BDOS call.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 3
lp:     PUSH BC
        LD   E, '+'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  BC
        DJNZ lp
        RET

lessons.title: Subroutines and the stack
lessons.summary: CALL, RET, PUSH, POP and keeping registers safe.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 1
        CALL double      ; A = 2
        CALL double      ; A = 4
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
double: ADD  A, A
        RET
sections.p: CALL label pushes the return address on the stack and jumps; RET pops it and goes back. A subroutine is just code that ends in RET. This one doubles A.

sections.code:
LD   BC, 1111h
        LD   DE, 2222h
        PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        POP  BC          ; BC = 2222h (DE went on last)
        POP  DE          ; DE = 1111h
sections.p: The stack grows downward in memory. PUSH puts a register pair on top and POP takes the top one off, so they come back in reverse order. Here the pops are crossed on purpose, which swaps the two pairs.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 'a'
        LD   B, 5
lp:     CALL putc
        INC  A
        DJNZ lp
        RET

putc:   PUSH AF          ; print the character in A
        PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        PUSH HL
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  HL
        POP  DE
        POP  BC
        POP  AF
        RET
sections.p: A routine that saves every register it uses can be called from anywhere without surprises. putc prints the character in A and keeps all registers, which makes the loop simple.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, m1
        CALL print
        LD   HL, m2
        CALL print
        RET

; print: HL = address of a $-ended string
print:  EX   DE, HL      ; the BDOS wants it in DE
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET

m1:     DB   'up the $'
m2:     DB   'tree$'
sections.p: Assembly has no parameters; you agree which registers carry what. Here print takes the address of a $-ended string in HL. Write that agreement in a comment above the routine.

RET pops whatever is on top of the stack. If a routine pushes something and forgets to pop it, RET jumps to that value instead of going home, and the program crashes. Every PUSH needs a matching POP on every path out.

practice.why: The stack is last in, first out: DE went on last, so it comes off first.
practice.q: You PUSH BC then PUSH DE. Which POP gets DE back?

practice.why: triple adds A twice and then the copy in B: 2 + 2 + 2.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 2
        CALL triple
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
triple: LD   B, A
        ADD  A, A
        ADD  A, B
        RET

practice.why: That return address is what RET pops so the program carries on after the CALL.
practice.q: What does CALL put on the stack?
options: The address of the next instruction
practice.answer: The address of the next instruction

practice.why: POP DE restores the pair saved earlier, so E is Y again.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   D, 'X'
        LD   E, 'Y'
        PUSH DE
        LD   D, 'A'
        LD   E, 'B'
        POP  DE
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: RET pops the top of the stack, which is now HL's old value, not the return address.
practice.q: A routine does PUSH HL but returns without POP HL. What happens at RET?
options: It jumps to the address that was in HL
practice.answer: It jumps to the address that was in HL

practice.why: Each CALL adds 3: 1 → 4 → 7.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 1
        CALL plus3
        CALL plus3
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
plus3:  ADD  A, 3
        RET

practice.why: POP DE restores the saved pair, so function 2 prints E, which is Q again.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   D, 'P'
        LD   E, 'Q'
        PUSH DE
        LD   D, 'R'
        LD   E, 'S'
        POP  DE
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

lessons.title: Memory, tables and strings
lessons.summary: Walking through memory with HL, lookup tables and LDIR.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, text
next:   LD   A, (HL)
        OR   A           ; the 0 at the end?
        RET  Z           ; then we are finished
        PUSH HL
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  HL
        INC  HL
        JR   next
text:   DB   'acorn', 0
sections.p: HL is the usual pointer. LD A, (HL) reads the byte it points at and INC HL moves to the next. Strings in assembly often end with a 0 byte; a loop prints until it finds it.
RET Z returns only if Z is set. That and RET NZ, RET C, RET NC make tidy exits from loops and routines. At the top level of a CP/M program a return ends the program.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   E, 3        ; which entry (counting from 0)
        LD   D, 0
        LD   HL, table
        ADD  HL, DE      ; HL = table + 3
        LD   E, (HL)
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
table:  DB   'ZOTF'      ; entries 0..3
sections.p: To turn a number into something else, keep the answers in a table and add the number to the table's address. ADD HL, DE does the indexing; D must be 0 so only E is added.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, buf
        LD   A, 'c'
        LD   (HL), A
        INC  HL
        LD   (HL), 'a'
        INC  HL
        LD   (HL), 't'
        INC  HL
        LD   (HL), '$'
        LD   DE, buf
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
buf:    DS   4
sections.p: LD (HL), A stores. DS n reserves n bytes of space for the program to fill in. Here the program writes three characters and a $ into a buffer, then prints it.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, src
        LD   DE, dst
        LD   BC, 6       ; five letters and the $
        LDIR
        LD   DE, dst
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
src:    DB   'copy!$'
dst:    DS   6
sections.p: LDIR copies BC bytes from the address in HL to the address in DE, moving both forward. It is a whole copy loop in one instruction.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, (count)
        ADD  A, 2
        LD   (count), A  ; count is now 7
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
count:  DB   5
sections.p: LD A, (count) and LD (count), A read and write a byte at a labelled address. That is how you keep a variable in memory when you run out of registers.

practice.why: HL starts at n; two INC HL move it to t (n, u, t).
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, word
        INC  HL
        INC  HL
        LD   E, (HL)
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
word:   DB   'nuts'

practice.why: LDIR copies from (HL) to (DE), counting BC down to 0.
practice.q: What does LDIR use as its byte count?

practice.why: Entries count from 0, so table + 1 is the second byte, b.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   E, 1
        LD   D, 0
        LD   HL, t
        ADD  HL, DE
        LD   E, (HL)
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
t:      DB   'abc'

practice.why: A conditional RET only returns when its condition holds.
practice.q: What does RET Z do if the Z flag is clear?

practice.why: The loop counts bytes until the 0: o, a and k.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, s
        LD   B, 0
cnt:    LD   A, (HL)
        OR   A
        JR   Z, done
        INC  B
        INC  HL
        JR   cnt
done:   LD   A, B
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
s:      DB   'oak', 0

practice.why: DS (define space) leaves room in the program for data written later.
HL starts at O; after printing, INC HL moves to K. PUSH/POP keep HL across the first CALL.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, w
        LD   E, (HL)
        PUSH HL
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  HL
        INC  HL
        LD   E, (HL)
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
w:      DB   'OK'

practice.why: LDIR copies four bytes including the $; function 9 prints up to that $.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   HL, src
        LD   DE, dst
        LD   BC, 4
        LDIR
        LD   DE, dst
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        RET
src:    DB   'hi!$'
dst:    DS   4

lessons.title: Bits and logic
lessons.summary: AND, OR, XOR, BIT/SET/RES and shifting.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 'q'
        AND  0DFh        ; clear bit 5: 'q' becomes 'Q'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        LD   A, 'Z'
        OR   20h         ; set bit 5: 'Z' becomes 'z'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: AND keeps only the bits set in both values, OR turns bits on, XOR flips them. A value used to pick bits is called a mask. In ASCII, lowercase and uppercase letters differ by one bit (20h), so clearing it uppercases a letter.

sections.code:
XOR  A           ; A = 0, Z set, carry clear
        XOR  0FFh        ; flips every bit: A = 255
sections.p: Any value XOR itself is 0, so XOR A is the shortest way to set A to 0 (and clear carry). You will see it everywhere in real Z80 code.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 5        ; 00000101b
        BIT  1, A        ; bit 1 is 0, so Z is set
        JR   Z, off
        LD   E, '1'
        JR   say
off:    LD   E, '0'
say:    LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: Bits are numbered 0 (the 1s place) to 7 (the 128s place). BIT n, r tests one bit and sets Z if it is 0. SET n, r turns it on and RES n, r turns it off. They work on any register or on (HL).

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 3
        SLA  B           ; 6
        SLA  B           ; 12
        SRL  B           ; 6
        LD   A, B
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET
sections.p: SLA r shifts every bit left, which doubles the number; the bit that falls out goes into carry. SRL r shifts right, halving it and dropping the remainder into carry. ADD A, A is a quick way to double A.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 0A5h     ; 10100101b
        LD   B, 8
bitlp:  RLCA             ; top bit into carry
        PUSH AF
        PUSH BC
        LD   E, '0'
        JR   NC, zero
        LD   E, '1'
zero:   LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  BC
        POP  AF
        DJNZ bitlp
        RET
sections.p: Shift A left eight times. Each time, the top bit drops into carry, and the program prints 0 or 1 depending on it. RLCA rotates A left, copying the top bit into both carry and bit 0.

practice.why: 11110000 AND 00111100 keeps only bits on in both: 00110000, which is 30h.
Clearing bit 5 (20h) turns a lowercase ASCII letter into uppercase.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 'm'
        AND  0DFh
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: Any value XOR itself is 0; XOR A is one byte, shorter than LD A, 0.
practice.q: Why do programmers write XOR A?
options: It sets A to 0 in one short instruction
It flips the sign of A
practice.answer: It sets A to 0 in one short instruction

practice.why: Each left shift doubles: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 1
        SLA  A
        SLA  A
        SLA  A
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: 4 is 00000100b: bit 2 is on, so BIT clears Z.
practice.q: After LD A, 4 then BIT 2, A, is Z set?

practice.why: Shifting right halves and drops the remainder: 9 → 4, with 1 in carry.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 9
        SRL  A
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: OR 20h leaves a lowercase letter alone; AND 0DFh then clears bit 5 to make A.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 'a'
        OR   20h
        AND  0DFh
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: SLA doubles: 3 becomes 6.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 3
        SLA  A
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

lessons.title: Printing numbers
lessons.summary: Turning a byte into decimal and hex digits, and multiplying.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 142
        CALL printd
        RET

; printd: print A (0-255) in decimal
printd: LD   D, 0        ; D = 1 once a digit has been printed
        LD   B, 100
        CALL digit
        LD   B, 10
        CALL digit
        ADD  A, '0'      ; units are always printed
        JP   putc
digit:  LD   C, '0'      ; count how many B's fit in A
dlp:    CP   B
        JR   C, dend
        SUB  B
        INC  C
        JR   dlp
dend:   PUSH AF
        LD   A, C
        CP   '0'
        JR   NZ, show
        BIT  0, D        ; a leading zero? skip it
        JR   Z, skip
show:   LD   D, 1
        CALL putc
skip:   POP  AF
        RET
putc:   PUSH AF          ; print the character in A
        PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        PUSH HL
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  HL
        POP  DE
        POP  BC
        POP  AF
        RET
sections.p: CP/M only prints characters, so a number has to be split into digits. For 0–255: count how many times 100 fits (subtract until it would go below 0), then 10, and what is left is the units. printd below skips the leading zeros.

printd ends with JP putc instead of CALL putc then RET. When a routine's last job is calling another routine, jumping to it lets that routine's RET return straight to the original caller. This is called a tail call.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 3Ch
        CALL printh
        RET

; printh: print A as two hex digits
printh: PUSH AF
        RRCA
        RRCA
        RRCA
        RRCA
        CALL nib         ; high half first
        POP  AF
nib:    AND  0Fh
        CP   10
        JR   C, dig
        ADD  A, 7        ; 10..15 become 'A'..'F'
dig:    ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        JP   5           ; the BDOS returns for us
sections.p: A byte is two hex digits, one per half (a nibble). Shift the top half down with four RRCAs, mask with AND 0Fh, and turn 0–15 into 0–9 or A–F. The letters start 7 places after '9'+1, hence the ADD A, 7.

sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 6        ; 6 x 7
        LD   C, 7
        XOR  A
mul:    ADD  A, C
        DJNZ mul         ; A = 42
        CALL printd
        RET

printd: LD   B, 10       ; print A (0-99) as two digits
        LD   C, '0'
tens:   CP   B
        JR   C, units
        SUB  B
        INC  C
        JR   tens
units:  PUSH AF
        LD   E, C
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  AF
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        JP   5
sections.p: The Z80 has no multiply instruction. The simple way is a loop that adds one number B times. Faster programs shift and add, but this is easy to check.

practice.why: Printing goes left to right, so the hundreds digit has to be worked out first.
practice.q: To print 142 one digit at a time, what do you find first?

practice.why: 10 fits into 37 three times before A drops below 10; the units (7) are never printed.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 37
        LD   B, 10
        LD   C, '0'
tens:   CP   B
        JR   C, show
        SUB  B
        INC  C
        JR   tens
show:   LD   E, C
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: 11 is not below 10, so 7 is added: 11 + 7 + '0' is the code for B.
practice.q: What is 0Bh as a printed hex digit?

practice.why: AND 0Fh keeps only the low nibble, which is 7.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 0A7h
        AND  0Fh
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: A tail call saves an instruction and a little stack; the result is the same.
practice.q: Why end printd with JP putc instead of CALL putc then RET?
options: putc's RET returns straight to printd's caller
JP is required after a CALL
practice.answer: putc's RET returns straight to printd's caller

practice.why: Adding 3 three times is 3 × 3.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 3
        XOR  A
mul:    ADD  A, 3
        DJNZ mul
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: Four RRCA moves bring the high nibble down; AND 0Fh keeps 3.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 37h
        RRCA
        RRCA
        RRCA
        RRCA
        AND  0Fh
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

practice.why: XOR A clears the total; three adds of C (3) make 9.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 3
        LD   C, 3
        XOR  A
mul:    ADD  A, C
        DJNZ mul
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        RET

lessons.title: Putting it together: FizzBuzz
lessons.summary: A whole program from the pieces: loops, compares, routines and printing.

sections.out:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
sections.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   A, 1
        LD   (n), A
        LD   A, 3
        LD   (three), A
        LD   A, 5
        LD   (five), A
loop:   LD   D, 0        ; D = 1 if a word was printed
        LD   HL, three
        DEC  (HL)
        JR   NZ, no3
        LD   (HL), 3
        LD   HL, fizz
        CALL print
        LD   D, 1
no3:    LD   HL, five
        DEC  (HL)
        JR   NZ, no5
        LD   (HL), 5
        LD   HL, buzz
        CALL print
        LD   D, 1
no5:    LD   A, D
        OR   A
        JR   NZ, eol
        LD   A, (n)
        CALL printd
eol:    LD   HL, crlf
        CALL print
        LD   A, (n)
        INC  A
        LD   (n), A
        CP   16          ; 1 to 15
        JR   NZ, loop
        RET

print:  PUSH DE          ; HL = $-ended string
        EX   DE, HL
        LD   C, 9
        CALL 5
        POP  DE
        RET
printd: LD   B, 10       ; A = 0-99
        LD   C, '0'
tens:   CP   B
        JR   C, units
        SUB  B
        INC  C
        JR   tens
units:  PUSH AF
        LD   A, C
        CP   '0'
        JR   Z, notens
        LD   E, C
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
notens: POP  AF
        ADD  A, '0'
        LD   E, A
        LD   C, 2
        JP   5

n:      DB   0
three:  DB   0
five:   DB   0
fizz:   DB   'Fizz$'
buzz:   DB   'Buzz$'
crlf:   DB   13, 10, '$'
sections.p: FizzBuzz prints the numbers from 1 up, but says Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5 and FizzBuzz for both. Instead of dividing, this version keeps two countdowns that reset to 3 and 5: when one reaches 0, it is time for that word.

sections.h: How to read a longer program
sections.p: Start at the labels: they name the parts. loop is one pass per number. three and five are the countdowns, kept in memory because there are not enough registers to go round. DEC (HL) counts a memory byte down and sets Z at 0, just as DEC B would. The routines at the bottom each save what they must and say in a comment what they expect.

You now know enough to read most Z80 listings. Good next steps: run these programs in RunCPM and change them; read a reference card for the full instruction set (exchange registers EXX, index registers IX/IY, block searches CPIR); then try a machine with a screen of its own, such as the ZX Spectrum in the Fuse emulator, where writing bytes to video memory draws pictures.

practice.why: The BDOS may change registers, and the program needs several values at once, so it parks them in memory.
practice.q: Why does this FizzBuzz keep its countdowns in memory?
options: There are not enough registers for everything
practice.answer: There are not enough registers for everything

practice.why: Brackets mean memory; DEC (HL) changes the byte and sets Z when it reaches 0.
options: Takes 1 from the byte HL points at
practice.answer: Takes 1 from the byte HL points at

practice.why: Every 15th pass is a multiple of both 3 and 5, so Fizz and then Buzz print.
practice.q: For the number 15, why are both words printed?
options: Both countdowns reach 0 on the same pass
FizzBuzz is stored as one word
practice.answer: Both countdowns reach 0 on the same pass

practice.why: The countdown in D hits 0 on passes 3 and 6, so ! prints twice.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 6
        LD   D, 3
lp:     DEC  D
        JR   NZ, skip
        LD   D, 3
        PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        LD   E, '!'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  DE
        POP  BC
skip:   DJNZ lp
        RET

practice.why: HL is the main address register: (HL) works with almost every instruction.
practice.q: Which register pair is most often used as a memory pointer?

practice.why: The countdown in D hits 0 on passes 2 and 4, so * prints twice in five loops.
practice.code:
ORG  100h
        LD   B, 5
        LD   D, 2
lp:     DEC  D
        JR   NZ, skip
        LD   D, 2
        PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        LD   E, '*'
        LD   C, 2
        CALL 5
        POP  DE
        POP  BC
skip:   DJNZ lp
        RET

practice.why: D starts at 0 each pass and becomes 1 if Fizz or Buzz printed, so the number can be skipped.
practice.q: In the FizzBuzz loop, what is D used for?
options: Remembering whether a word was printed this pass
practice.answer: Remembering whether a word was printed this pass
